title: Lesson 10: The Circle of Fifths on the Guitar
intro: The circle of fifths arranges the twelve keys so that each is a fifth from its neighbours (see Key Signatures and the Circle of Fifths (#/arts/music-theory/scales-and-keys/circle-of-fifths)). On the guitar the circle is not just a diagram: a fifth and a fourth are fixed shapes on the neck, so you can walk the whole circle with two barre-chord shapes, and the chords of any key sit in one small patch of frets.

items: See where a fifth and a fourth are on the fretboard.
Walk all twelve keys around the circle with E-shape and A-shape barre chords.
Use the circle to find the I, IV and V chords, the relative minor and the progressions that follow the circle.
Lesson 3 (notes on strings 6 and 5), Lesson 4 (interval shapes) and Lesson 5 (barre chords).

blocks.alt: A circle with the twelve major keys around the outside, C at the top, then G, D, A, E, B, F♯/G♭, D♭, A♭, E♭, B♭ and F going clockwise; the relative minor keys inside and the number of sharps or flats beside each.
blocks.caption: The circle of fifths. Clockwise is up a fifth (one more sharp); anticlockwise is up a fourth (one more flat). Inside each key is its relative minor.

blocks.text: Find a fifth and a fourth on the neck

items: Step 1. Put finger 1 on string 6 fret 3 (G). One string up and two frets higher, string 5 fret 5, is D: a perfect fifth above G. Moving one step clockwise on the circle is this shape: next string, two frets up.

Step 2. Go back to G on string 6 fret 3. The same fret on string 5 is C: a perfect fourth above G. Moving one step anticlockwise (one sharp fewer, or one flat more) is this shape: next string, same fret.
Step 3. On one string a fifth is 7 frets up (or 5 frets down) and a fourth is 5 frets up. Those are the same notes as the cross-string shapes, an octave apart.
Step 4. Step through the example: root, fifth, root, fourth.

widget.title: Fifth and fourth from G (string 6, fret 3)

examples.label: G → C (fourth: next string, same fret)

blocks.text: Walk the whole circle with two barre shapes

items: Step 1. Start on C with the A-shape barre at fret 3 (x-3-5-5-5-3, root on string 5).
Step 2. One step clockwise is G. Its root is a fifth above C: on string 6 the G is at fret 3, the same fret. Play the E-shape barre there (3-5-5-4-3-3).
Step 3. Next is D: root on string 5 fret 5 (two frets up). A-shape at fret 5. Then A: E-shape at fret 5.

Step 4. The pattern repeats: A shape, E shape at the same fret, then both two frets higher. C (A, 3), G (E, 3), D (A, 5), A (E, 5), E (A, 7), B (E, 7), F♯ (A, 9), C♯/D♭ (E, 9), A♭ (A, 11), E♭ (E, 11), B♭ (A, 1 or 13), F (E, 1 or 13), and back to C.
Step 5. Step through the example below and say each key name and its number of sharps or flats as you play: C 0, G 1♯, D 2♯, A 3♯, E 4♯, B 5♯, F♯ 6♯ (= G♭ 6♭), D♭ 5♭, A♭ 4♭, E♭ 3♭, B♭ 2♭, F 1♭.

widget.title: The circle of fifths, one key per step

blocks.text: I, IV and V are neighbours

items: Step 1. Any key's three main chords (I, IV, V; see Harmony (#/arts/music-theory/harmony)) are its own key and the two keys either side of it on the circle: in G, they are C (one step anticlockwise), G and D (one step clockwise).

Step 2. On the neck they form a fixed block: put the I chord's root on string 6 (E shape). The IV is an A-shape chord at the same fret, the V an A-shape chord two frets higher. In G: G at fret 3 (E shape), C at fret 3 (A shape), D at fret 5 (A shape).
Step 3. Move the block to any fret and you have I, IV and V of a new key: at fret 5 it is A, D and E; at fret 8 it is C, F and G.

Step 4. With the I chord as an A shape instead (root on string 5 at fret f), the V is the E-shape chord at the same fret and the IV is the E-shape chord two frets lower. In C (A shape, fret 3): G (E shape, fret 3) and F (E shape, fret 1).

widget.title: I–IV–V–I as one block of frets

examples.label: Same block at fret 5: A major

items: Step 1. Many progressions move anticlockwise round the circle, each root a fifth below the last: vi–ii–V–I. In G: Em – Am – D – G. Play them as open chords: 022000, x02210, xx0232, 320003.

Step 2. Make each chord a dominant seventh and the pull gets stronger: E7 – A7 – D7 – G (020100, x02020, xx0212, 320003). This chain of secondary dominants is the 'ragtime' progression of countless old songs (see Secondary Dominants (#/arts/music-theory/harmony/secondary-dominants)).

Step 3. The full diatonic circle in G: G – C – F♯° – Bm – Em – Am – D – G. Every chord's root is a fourth above the last (a fifth below); C to F♯ is the one augmented fourth, because the circle has to stay inside the key.

examples.label: Dominant chain: E7 – A7 – D7 – G

blocks.text: Relative minors, guitar keys and the capo

items: Step 1. Every major key shares its notes with a minor key three frets lower (the inner ring of the circle). On the neck: move the root down three frets on the same string. C on string 5 fret 3 → A on the open string 5: A minor. G on string 6 fret 3 → open E: E minor.
Step 2. The guitar's open strings favour the sharp side of the circle: E, A, D and G (and C) are the easy open-chord keys. Flat keys (F, B♭, E♭, A♭) need barre chords or a capo.
Step 3. Capo arithmetic counts semitones: each capo fret raises the key by one semitone, so G shapes with a capo at 3 sound in B♭, C shapes at 3 in E♭, D shapes at 1 in E♭, E shapes at 1 in F.
3 min: root walk round the circle on strings 5 and 6, saying each key name.
4 min: the barre-chord walk, one chord per beat at 60 BPM, then reversed (anticlockwise: C, F, B♭, E♭...).
3 min: the I–IV–V block at frets 3, 5, 7 and 8; name the key each time.
3 min: E7 – A7 – D7 – G, then Em – Am – D – G.

blocks.title: Next key
blocks.text: You are playing an E-shape A major at fret 5. Where is the next key clockwise, and which shape?
solution: Clockwise from A is E (a fifth up). Its root is on string 5 fret 7 (next string, two frets up): A-shape E major at fret 7, x-7-9-9-9-7.
blocks.answer: E major, A shape at fret 7

blocks.title: Block
blocks.text: Which three chords does the I–IV–V block give with the E-shape root at fret 8?
solution: String 6 fret 8 is C: I = C (E shape, fret 8), IV = F (A shape, fret 8), V = G (A shape, fret 10).

blocks.title: Relative minor
blocks.text: What is the relative minor of D major, and where is its root if D is on string 5 fret 5?
solution: Three frets lower on the same string: string 5 fret 2 is B. B minor.
